subject: chemistry
question_text: Explain the formation of coordinate covalent bond with one example.

verification.note: Chapter 3 is sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack chemistry section (book pp.56-61), which prints the question, its star rank and a model answer. Only ONE source book is held for chemistry — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only — so the two-book union check is PENDING a second chemistry source. The 1+1+1+1 mark split is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. The book's example line is garbled in print ('Ex H F N atoms of ammonia B Boron trifluoride Donor acceptor'); the intended example is ammonia with boron trifluoride, written out fully on the card as H₃N → BF₃.

steps.label: Definition
lines: Coordinate covalent bond: a covalent bond
in which the shared pair of electrons is
contributed by only ONE of the two bonded
atoms.
Once formed, it is identical to a normal
covalent bond.
steps.why: The single phrase that defines this bond is contributed by only one atom — everything else about it is ordinary covalent sharing.
common_mistakes: Writing that each atom gives one electron. That is a normal covalent bond; here one atom gives BOTH.
Calling it an ionic bond. No electron is transferred; the pair is shared.
steps.memory_tip: Normal covalent: one electron each. Coordinate: both electrons from one atom.
steps.margin_note: Underline only one — it is the defining phrase.

steps.label: Donor and acceptor
lines: Donor: the atom that contributes the
electron pair. It must have a lone pair.
Acceptor: the atom that receives the pair.
It must have a vacant orbital.
The bond is written as an arrow from the
donor to the acceptor.
steps.why: The two conditions — a lone pair on one side and a vacant orbital on the other — are what make the bond possible, so they are named with the two terms.
common_mistakes: Swapping the terms: the donor has the lone pair, the acceptor has the vacant orbital.
Writing the arrow from acceptor to donor. The arrow follows the electron pair.
steps.memory_tip: Donor gives from its lone pair; acceptor has the empty orbital that receives it.
steps.margin_note: Two definitions, one line each, then the arrow rule.

steps.label: The example
lines: Example — ammonia with boron trifluoride:
In NH₃ the N atom has one lone pair.
In BF₃ the B atom has a vacant orbital
(only six electrons around B).
N donates its lone pair into the vacant
orbital of B.
steps.why: The example works because each molecule supplies exactly one requirement: NH₃ the lone pair, BF₃ the vacant orbital.
common_mistakes: Saying BF₃ donates. Boron is electron-deficient; it ACCEPTS the pair.
Forgetting to say why BF₃ can accept — boron has only six electrons around it.
steps.memory_tip: NH₃ has the pair, BF₃ has the space.
steps.margin_note: NH₄⁺ (NH₃ with H⁺) is an accepted alternative example.

steps.label: The arrow notation
lines: The arrow starts at the donor N and points
to the acceptor B, showing that both
electrons of the shared pair came from N.
steps.why: The arrow is the notation the examiner checks: it records which atom gave the pair, which a plain dash cannot show.
common_mistakes: Writing H₃N−BF₃ with a plain dash. The dash loses the donor information; the arrow is required.
steps.memory_tip: The arrow points the way the electron pair went: from N to B.
steps.margin_note: Box the formula with the arrow — it is the answer in one line.

insider_note: The arrow from donor to acceptor is the notation the examiner looks for — write H₃N → BF₃ with the arrow, never a plain dash.
